'''Sandra Steingraber''' (born 1959) is an American [[biologist]], author, and [[cancer survivor]]. Steingraber writes and lectures on the [[natural environment|environment]]al factors that contribute to reproductive health problems and environmental links to cancer.

==Early life==
Steingraber was adopted as an infant. She grew up and spent most of her childhood in [[Tazewell County, Illinois]]. Her mother was a [[microbiologist]] and her father was a community college professor.<ref>{{cite book | author= Sandra Steingraber | title=Having Faith: an Ecologist's Journey to Motherhood | url= https://archive.org/details/havingfaithecol100stei | url-access= registration | year=2001 | publisher=Perseus| isbn=9780738204673 }}</ref> Her parents inculcated in her an interest in [[sustainable development]] and [[organic agriculture]] from a young age.<ref>{{cite web| title=The Ecology of Pizza| author=Sandra Steingraber| url=http://www.theorganicreport.com/pages/318_the_ecology_of_pizza_entire_19_pages_.cfm| access-date=2006-08-31| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060908193435/http://www.theorganicreport.com/pages/318_the_ecology_of_pizza_entire_19_pages_.cfm| archive-date=September 8, 2006| df=mdy-all}}</ref>

In her 20s, Steingraber developed [[bladder cancer]].<ref name="steingraber.com">{{cite web|title=About the Author |author=Sandra Steingraber |url=http://www.steingraber.com/index.html |access-date=2009-11-27 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090130041901/http://steingraber.com/index.html |archive-date=January 30, 2009 }}</ref> In several of her books, she describes an apparent [[cancer cluster]] in her hometown and within her family.<ref>{{cite book | author= Sandra Steingraber | title=Living Downstream: an Ecologist Looks at Cancer and the Environment | url= https://archive.org/details/livingdownstream00stei_1 | url-access= registration | year=1997 | publisher=Addison-Wesley| isbn=9780201483031 }}</ref>

After her cancer went into [[remission (medicine)|remission]], Steingraber completed her undergraduate degree in [[biology]] from [[Illinois Wesleyan University]]. She worked for several years as a field researcher, eventually earning her doctorate in biology from the [[University of Michigan]]. Steingraber also holds a master's degree in English from [[Illinois State University]].

== Career ==
Steingraber has been on faculty at [[Cornell University]], and is a Distinguished Visiting Scholar at the Division of Interdisciplinary and International Studies at [[Ithaca College]], in [[Ithaca, New York]].<ref name="steingraber.com" /> She held visiting fellowships at the [[University of Illinois]], [[Radcliffe College|Radcliffe/Harvard]], and [[Northeastern University]], and served on President [[Bill Clinton]]'s National Action Plan on Breast Cancer.<ref>{{cite web | title=Sandra Steingraber | author=Eco Mama|url=http://www.indiebound.org/author-interviews/steingraber| access-date=2009-11-27}}</ref>

== Activism ==

===''Living Downstream''===
In her 1997 book, ''Living Downstream'', Steingraber blends anecdotes and descriptions of industrial and [[agricultural pollution]] with data from scientific and medical literature to assess the relationship between environmental factors and cancer. Steingraber criticizes the imbalance between funding devoted to studies of genetic predisposition to cancer versus studies of environmental contributions. The book claims that while we can do little to change our genetic inheritance, much can be done to reduce human exposure to environmental [[carcinogens]].<ref>{{cite book | first=Thomas | last=Easton | year=2009 | title=Sources: Environmental Studies|volume= 3| page=157}}</ref>

Her work ''Living Downstream: An Ecologist Looks at Cancer and the Environment'', reflects the ideals that [[Rachel Carson]] expressed in her seminal book, ''[[Silent Spring]]''.  Carson discusses a woman with bladder cancer and investigates research on how and why cancer is linked to the environment. Steingraber stresses issues such as how chemical pesticides find their way into human bodies. She states, "in 1996 a study investigated six-fold excess of bladder cancer among workers exposed years before to [[o-toluidine]] and [[aniline]] in the rubber chemicals department of a manufacturing plant in upstate New York. Levels of these contaminants are now well within their legal workplace limits and yet blood and urine samples collected from current employees were found to contain substantial numbers of DNA [[adducts]] and detectable levels of o-toluidine and aniline."

<blockquote>
"To the 89 percent of Illinois that is farmland, an estimated 54 million pounds of synthetic pesticides are applied each year. Introduced into Illinois at the end of World War II, these chemical poisons quietly familiarized themselves with the landscape. In 1950, less than 10 percent of cornfields were sprayed with pesticides. In 1993, 99 percent were chemically treated," (page 5).
</blockquote>

''Living Downstream'' is the basis for a documentary by The People's Picture Company<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.theppcinc.com/|title=PPC - Welcome!}}</ref> that chronicles Steingraber's struggles as a cancer survivor and her contributions as an ecologist and cancer prevention activist.

On March 18, 2013, Steingraber was arrested along with nine other protesters for blocking the entrance to the [[Inergy]] [[natural gas]] facility near [[Ithaca, New York|Ithaca]] to protest "the industrialization of the Finger Lakes." After refusing to pay a fine, Steingraber and two other members of the "Seneca Lake 12" received 15-day sentences. Steingraber served 10 days in the [[Chemung County, New York|Chemung County]] jail in the city of [[Elmira, New York|Elmira]] before her release.

On October 29, 2014, while participating in the [[civil disobedience]] campaign, called We Are Seneca Lake, Steingraber was arrested again with nine other protestors at the gates of Crestwood Midstream (formerly Inergy) for trespassing and blocking a chemical truck, which resulted in an additional charge of disorderly conduct. On November 19, in the Town of Reading Court, she was sentenced to 15-days in jail after refusing to pay her fine. She served 8-days in the Chemung County jail and was released. Steingraber detailed her experience in an ''Ecowatch'' article, "Why I am in Jail."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ecowatch.com/2014/11/21/sandra-steingraber-why-im-in-jail/|title=Sandra Steingraber: Why I am in Jail|author=Sandra Steingraber|work=EcoWatch|date=November 21, 2014 }}</ref>

=== Unfractured ===
Steingraber was the subject of the 2018 documentary, ''Unfractured''.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.desmogblog.com/2018/01/12/unfractured-documentary-sandra-steingraber-fracking|title=Unfractured: A Documentary on Activism, Family and the Fight Against Fracking|last=Mikulka|first=Justin|date=2018-01-12|work=DeSmogBlog|access-date=2018-09-30|language=en}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Steingraber lives in [[Trumansburg, New York]] with her husband Jeff de Castro, a sculptor and [[art restoration]] specialist, with their two children.<ref>{{cite press release|title=Sandra Steingraber Arrested with Local Residents and Students in Blockade of Watkins Glen, NY Natural Gas Storage Facility|date=18 March 2013|publisher=Our Future is Unfractured|url=http://ourfutureisunfractured.wordpress.com/press-release/|access-date=2014-03-10}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://steingraber.com/bio/|title=Bio|last=Steingraber|first=Sandra|work=Sandra Steingraber|access-date=10 March 2014|archive-date=February 14, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140214152119/http://steingraber.com/bio/|url-status=dead}}</ref> In July 2019, Sandra Steingraber announced in an essay that she was gay, timing her announcement to coincide with LGBT STEM day.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2019-07-05|title=Always Knew I Was Adopted; Just Found Out I'm Gay|url=https://www.terrain.org/2019/guest-editorial/just-found-out-im-gay/|access-date=2020-11-20|website=Terrain.org|language=en-US}}</ref>

== Bibliography ==

* ''The Spoils of Famine: Ethiopian Famine Policy and Peasant Agriculture (Cultural Survival Report 25)'' (1988, co-author), which raised issues of ecology and human rights in Africa.
* ''Post-diagnosis'' (1995), a volume of poetry on living with cancer.
* ''Living Downstream: An Ecologist Looks at Cancer and the Environment'' (1997), which proposed a relationship between cancer registry data and [[Toxics Release Inventory]] data.
* ''Having Faith: An Ecologist's Journey to Motherhood'' (2001), which explored fetal toxicology and genetics with respect to Steingraber's own pregnancy.
* ''The Falling Age of Puberty in U.S. Girls: what we know, what we need to know'' (2007), which reviews the epidemiology and etiology of the acceleration of puberty among girls in the USA.
* ''Raising Elijah: Protecting Our Children in an Age of Environmental Crisis'' (2011, [[Merloyd Lawrence Books]]) {{ISBN|978-0-7382-1399-6}}

* 1997 – Named a Ms. Magazine Woman of the Year.<ref name="Sandra Steingraber">{{cite web | title=About the Author | author=Sandra Steingraber | url=http://steingraber.com/bio/ | access-date=2014-02-16 | archive-date=February 14, 2014 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140214152119/http://steingraber.com/bio/ | url-status=dead }}</ref>
* 1998 – First annual Altman Award for "the inspiring and poetic use of science to elucidate the causes of cancer," from the Jenifer Altman Foundation
* 1998 – Will Solimene Award for "excellence in medical communication" from the New England chapter of the American Medical Writers Association.<ref name="Sandra Steingraber"/>
* 1999 – Sierra Club heralded Steingraber as "the new [[Rachel Carson]]."<ref name="Sandra Steingraber"/>
* 2001 – Biennial Rachel Carson Leadership Award from [[Chatham College]], [[Rachel Carson]]'s alma mater.<ref>{{cite web| title=A Talk with Dr. Sandra Steingraber| author=The O'Mama Report| url=http://www.theorganicreport.com/pages/45_a_talk_with_dr_sandra_steingraber.cfm| access-date=2009-11-27| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090527000725/http://www.theorganicreport.com/pages/45_a_talk_with_dr_sandra_steingraber.cfm| archive-date=May 27, 2009| df=mdy-all}}</ref>
* 2006 – Received the Breast Cancer Fund's "Hero Award" along with [[Teresa Heinz Kerry]]. In recognition to honor and publicly thank those who have significantly helped advance our mission to identify and eliminate the environmental—and preventable—causes of breast cancer.<ref>{{cite web| title=Breast Cancer Fund's Annual Heroes Tribute – A History| author=The Breast Cancer Fund| url=http://www.breastcancerfund.org/community/heroes.html| access-date=2014-02-16| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222214528/http://www.breastcancerfund.org/community/heroes.html| archive-date=February 22, 2014| df=mdy-all}}</ref>
* 2008 – Honorary [[Doctor of Letters]] (D.Litt.) awarded by [[Lycoming College]], [[Williamsport, PA]], in recognition of excellence in research and writing.
* 2010 – Named one of the "25 Visionaries Who Are Changing Your World" by [[Utne Reader]] magazine.<ref name="utne">{{cite web|title=Sandra Steingraber: Her Body, Their Chemicals|url=http://www.utne.com/Politics/Utne-Reader-Visionaries-Sandra-Steingraber-Organic-Manifesto.aspx|access-date=October 19, 2010}}</ref>
* 2012 – Received the 17th Annual [[Heinz Award]] with special focus on the environment<ref>{{cite web|title=The Heinz Awards: Sandra Steingraber|url=http://www.heinzawards.net/recipients/sandra-steingraber|website=The Heinz Awards|access-date=August 26, 2016}}</ref><ref name= sandranancy>{{Citation

 | newspaper =[[Harvard Magazine]]
 | date = September 14, 2011
 | url = http://harvardmagazine.com/2011/09/nancy-knowlton-sandra-steingraber-heinz-awards
 | access-date = 2013-05-17}}</ref>
* 2013 – Received the Doctor of Humane Letters honorary degree. award by SUNY college of Environmental Science & Forestry<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.esf.edu/communications/view.asp?newsID=2260|title=Honoree Sets Path for Grads to Improve Their World|author=SUNY-ESF Office of Communications|work=SUNY-ESF}}</ref>
* 2015 – Received the American Ethical Union's Elliott-Black Award "for protecting our planet and informing others on how to get active ..."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://aeu.org/2015/03/elliott-black-award-goes-to-sandra-steingraber/|title=American Ethical Union » Elliott-Black Award goes to Dr. Sandra Steingraber|work=American Ethical Union}}</ref>
* 2015 - Received Breast Cancer Action's "Barbara Brenner Hell Raiser Award" for shining "a light on the links between toxic chemicals and breast cancer" and for bringing her "academic knowledge to the real world through political advocacy and direct action."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://bcaction.org/2015/08/20/breast-cancer-action-honors-acclaimed-ecologist-dr-sandra-steingraber-with-barbara-brenner-hell-raiser-award/|title=Breast Cancer Action Honors Acclaimed Ecologist Dr. Sandra Steingraber With Barbara Brenner Hell Raiser Award|work=Breast Cancer Action|date=August 21, 2015 }}</ref>
